lesson.title: Rosa Parks: The Deliberate Defiance Behind a Famous Arrest
lesson.summary: Rosa Parks is often remembered simply as a tired seamstress who refused to move, but she was in fact a trained, experienced civil rights organizer whose act of defiance was part of a long running strategy to challenge segregation in court.
lesson.body:
The popular story of Rosa Parks, that she was simply a tired seamstress who spontaneously refused to give up her bus seat one evening, captures a small part of the truth but leaves out most of it. Parks was indeed tired that day, as she said herself, tired of the daily indignity of segregation, but her refusal on December 1, 1955, was the act of a seasoned activist, not a stranger to protest.

Born in Tuskegee, Alabama, in 1913, Parks had been involved in civil rights work for over a decade before her famous arrest. She served as secretary of the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP starting in 1943, working closely alongside chapter president E. D. Nixon, a longtime labor and civil rights organizer. In that role she documented cases of racial violence and abuse, including assaults against Black women, and helped investigate cases that rarely received attention from white authorities. In the summer of 1955, just months before her arrest, she attended a workshop at the Highlander Folk School in Monteagle, Tennessee, a training center for labor and civil rights organizers that taught strategies for nonviolent resistance and desegregation campaigns.

Parks was also not the first Montgomery resident arrested for refusing to give up a bus seat. In March 1955, a fifteen year old student named Claudette Colvin was arrested for the same act of defiance, but local NAACP leaders, weighing how the case might be received, decided a teenager was not the ideal figure to build a legal challenge around at that moment. Parks, an adult with an established reputation in the community and years of organizing experience, made a far stronger public case, and local activists were ready to act quickly once she was arrested. Colvin was not forgotten, however: she later served as one of the plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the federal lawsuit that ultimately ended Montgomery's bus segregation.

None of this diminishes the courage of what Parks did. Refusing to move still meant risking arrest, and possibly violence, under a legal system built to punish exactly that kind of defiance. What it changes is the story's meaning. Rosa Parks's arrest was not an isolated accident that happened to spark a movement, but the deliberate act of an experienced organizer that a prepared network of activists, including Jo Ann Robinson and the Women's Political Council, was ready to turn into the sustained protest that became the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
